rv.q: Hill-Gibbins’s production is a satisfyingly dagger-sharp provocation for our own age of political uncertainty and civil unrest.
This is a brilliant act of butchery, leaving just the leanest, bloodiest, choicest cuts.

Set within the candlelit confines of the Sam Wanamaker Playhouse, director Joe Hill-Gibbins’ feverish 90-minute adaptation reintroduces some of that fascinating historical weirdness to powerful effect.
In its way, this is a masterpiece of editing and distillation, and a fresh take on a play that proves surprisingly malleable.
More a muddle than a triumph, it may prove a confusing introduction to Shakespeare; but it’s a visually memorable one nonetheless.

It's a fresh, unexpected, and powerful take on Julius Caesar which maps out perfectly into an honest and emotional exploration of young people who are trying to figure out who they want to be in a world that seems weighted against him.
Lend your ears to Julius Caesar Remixed, a worthy 90 minutes of inspiring, entertaining and relevant theatre.
Joe Hill-Gibbins’ intensely intimate production of Shakespeare’s thriller finds a fitting home here...

The show is an entertaining spectacle that is deprived of consistent characters, clear politics or the stunning clarity of some of the language, all of which has been replaced by a dark, harsh, expressionist visual intensity, perhaps meant to convey the fear, horror and discontent of the current world we endure.
On the Sam Wanamaker stage, this is a play all about people, driving themselves mad with their own mistrust and ambition.
Hill-Gibbins has successfully created an atmosphere of dread and rebellion, but there is a distinct void where some substance ought to be.
The piece works brilliantly as a gripping, darkly atmospheric rollercoaster ride into betrayal, rabble-rousing, and brutal comeuppance.
Julius Caesar Remixed powerfully reimagines Shakespeare, resulting in an astounding symphony of vibrancy and sensitivity.
It’s intense and intimate, a reversal of the broad, public spectacle we might associate with this play.
It’s a brilliant performance that will give you goosebumps.
This production of Julius Caesar certainly earns its place among Shakespearean revivals in London this winter.
This gripping and grounded production proves why there is no better place to watch the Bard's plays.
But to achieve that, it ultimately sacrifices some of the poetry while individual character motivation becomes a little unstuck along the way.
Joe Hill-Gibbins's heavy trimming sacrifices pathos and profundity for thrill and accessibility.

cn.t: Critics find this stripped-back, four-actor Julius Caesar visually arresting and bracingly tense, though some feel the radical condensation sacrifices emotional depth. Inventive staging wins praise; opinions split on whether style trumps substance.
